postTitle: Cash Management: Where to Hold Your Cash
topic: Cash has three jobs, and each job belongs in a different kind of account

assumptions.notes: Eva holds €30,000 of cash, all in a current account at 0%. Costs €2,500 a month. Split: spending 1 month = €2,500; safety buffer 5 months = €12,500 (inside the common 3 to 6 month guideline); flat deposit due in about 3 years = €15,000. Total €30,000. At 2% inflation, €30,000 at 0% loses 2% × €30,000 = €600 of purchasing power a year (same example as the blog post). If only the €2,500 spending bucket sits at 0%: 2% × €2,500 = €50 a year, assuming the other two buckets roughly keep pace with inflation. Illustrative.

beats.narration: Job one is spending. About one month of costs, for bills and daily life. A current account usually fits that.
Job two is the safety buffer. A common guideline is three to six months of costs, in savings or a money market fund.
Job three is money with a date. Her flat deposit, in about three years. That can sit in Treasury bills or term deposits.
At two percent inflation, all of it at zero costs her about six hundred euros a year. Split by job, only the spending bucket sits at zero. About fifty.
So for every euro of cash, ask one question. When might I need it?

caption.instagram:
If all your cash sits in one account, it may be doing two of its three jobs poorly.

Eva keeps all €30,000 of her cash in her current account, at 0%. Split by job: one month of costs for spending, €2,500; a safety buffer of five months, €12,500; and €15,000 for a flat deposit in about three years. At 2% inflation, all of it at 0% costs her about €600 of purchasing power a year. Split by job, only the spending bucket sits at 0%: about €50, if the rest roughly keeps pace with inflation.

A common way to sort cash is by when it might be needed. This month: often a current account. In an emergency: often savings or a money market fund. In 2 to 5 years: often Treasury bills or term deposits.
